title: Inside attention
overview: Point a query. Watch the weights move. Break the mask. Follow the exact source behind each mechanism.

scenes.title: Start with the job the machine is doing
scenes.explanation: Think of the encoder as producing a contextual table: one numeric vector for each input position, updated using the other input positions. The decoder reads that table and the output prefix, then predicts one next symbol. The original paper uses six layers in each stack. Within a layer, attention mixes information between positions; the feed-forward network transforms each position. Residual connections and normalization keep an additional path around each sublayer. Move the output-step control to reveal how the known prefix grows. Play follows one illustrative route through the components.

assumptions: The token sequence and moving pulse illustrate information flow; this scene does not run a trained Transformer or compute next-token probabilities.
Each large block compresses a stack of six layers from the paper. The original implementation also includes learned projections, residual connections, normalization, and output softmax.
The decoder sees shifted output embeddings. During training the mask permits parallel processing while withholding each row’s future answers.

steps.title: Represent the input
steps.text: Each input token becomes a vector with position information.

steps.title: Contextualize it
steps.text: The encoder updates each position using information from the input sequence.

steps.title: Use the prefix and source
steps.text: The decoder’s masked attention handles the output prefix; cross-attention reads encoder keys and values.

steps.title: Predict, then repeat
steps.text: A next-token distribution produces the next symbol. The enlarged prefix is input to the following generation step.

scenes.title: A query is a direction. Attention is a mixture.
scenes.explanation: A query is a numeric request for relevant information. Each key is compared with it by a dot product; each associated value is the payload available to mix into the answer. In this toy example the query has two components, the three keys are shown explicitly, and the payloads are single numbers. Change either query component and follow the resulting scores, softmax weights and weighted value. Turning on the paper’s square-root scaling divides scores by sqrt(2). Temperature is an extra exploration control: raising it spreads the weights. This makes the operation in softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V tangible without pretending the weights are statements of truth. The moving marker traces the computation from query and keys through scores, normalized weights and the weighted answer.

scenes.alt_text: The left plane shows three fixed blue keys and a gold query vector. The first matrix row shows scaled dot products; the second row shows normalized weights. A final readout computes the weighted sum of scalar values 2, 8 and -2. The full numerical readout is available below the stage.
assumptions: The displayed keys, values, query and score magnitudes are illustrative, not measured parameters from the paper.
The toy key dimension is two. Changing the score-magnitude control multiplies dot products; it does not change dimensionality.
Temperature is a demonstration extension, not an extra parameter in the paper’s displayed base equation.
Softmax weights are mixing coefficients. A concentrated distribution does not by itself establish understanding or correctness.

reveal.title: Key 1
reveal.text: Key [1,0] responds to the first query component. Its scalar value is 2.

reveal.title: Key 2
reveal.text: Key [0,1] responds to the second component. Its scalar value is 8.

reveal.title: Key 3
reveal.text: Key [1,1] matches both positive components. Its scalar value is -2: a strong match need not have a positive payload.

reveal.title: Move the query
reveal.text: Change q₁ and q₂. The gold direction changes; each key's dot product changes with it. Keys are fixed in this example.

reveal.title: Before softmax
reveal.text: These are scaled query-key dot products. The query and keys have two components; dividing by √2 controls their scale.

reveal.title: A row of attention
reveal.text: Exponentiate and normalize. Each weight is nonnegative and the row sums to one. Brightness is proportional to that contribution.

objects.text: Weights choose how much. Values supply what.

steps.title: Compute compatibility
steps.text: For keys [1,0], [0,1], and [1,1], the unscaled dot products are q₁, q₂, and q₁+q₂, multiplied here by the magnitude control.

steps.title: Control score scale
steps.text: The paper divides by the square root of key dimension. Its variance argument assumes independent components with zero mean and unit variance.

steps.title: Normalize and mix
steps.text: Exponentiate and normalize the scores, then use those weights to combine values. Changing V would change the answer without changing the compatibility weights.

steps.title: Investigate concentration
steps.text: Increase score magnitude and compare scaled with unscaled weights. Then increase temperature and notice that the answer becomes a broader mixture.

presets.title: No preferred direction
presets.description: A zero query gives every key the same score and an equal share.

presets.title: Favor the first axis
presets.description: The query points toward keys 1 and 3; their equal dot products produce equal weights.

presets.title: Oppose the diagonal
presets.description: The third key now points against the query. Its negative value receives little weight.

presets.title: Make the choice sharp
presets.description: Low temperature concentrates weight on the largest score; this is an exploratory intervention.

scenes.title: Show exactly what a causal mask prevents
scenes.explanation: The decoder may process many training positions at once, but each position must only use the allowed prefix. The paper sets forbidden pre-softmax scores to negative infinity. Their exponentials are exactly zero, so forbidden values contribute nothing. Here each label is a shifted decoder input: row 2 can use <start> and The while predicting the next output. Leave row 2 selected and change key 3’s score or payload. With masking enabled the output stays the same. Disable the mask and the future information can change the output. That is the leakage the mask prevents.

scenes.alt_text: A four-by-four matrix displays query rows and key columns. With masking enabled, entries above the diagonal are zero. The selected row is emphasized. Readouts report future attention mass, the third key weight and the resulting weighted value.
assumptions: The numeric scores and values are illustrative scalar payloads, not a language model’s probabilities or trained states.
This implementation uses an exact zero numerator for masked positions, mathematically equivalent to exponentiating a negative-infinity score.
Input labels are shifted relative to output targets; the permitted diagonal is not permission to read the answer being predicted.

objects.text: THE FUTURE CAN BE ATTRACTIVE. IT STILL GETS ZERO.

reveal.title: Causal attention matrix
reveal.text: A query row may read itself and earlier decoder input positions. Masking removes later columns before normalization. This matrix uses the same toy key scores in every row to isolate that effect.

objects.text: Try to make a future token matter. Then switch the mask off.
Rows are queries. Columns are available keys.

steps.title: Read only the prefix
steps.text: With row 2 selected, keys 3 and 4 are excluded. Their weights are exactly zero.

steps.title: Try to leak information
steps.text: Change key 3’s score and value. With the mask on, neither can affect this row’s weighted output. The cursor visits each key; the numeric weights show whether its payload can enter the answer.

steps.title: Remove the protection
steps.text: Switch the mask off. Now a future key can acquire weight and inject its payload into the current output.

presets.title: Seal the future
presets.description: A very attractive future key still contributes exactly zero.

presets.title: Break the seal
presets.description: The same future key becomes visible when the mask is disabled.

presets.title: Move forward in time
presets.description: By row 3, key 3 is available and can contribute legitimately.

scenes.title: Several views can survive the same lookup
scenes.explanation: One attention head returns one weighted mixture. The paper projects queries, keys and values through different learned matrices and runs attention in parallel. The separate results are concatenated and projected again. In this two-head toy, changing the separation control rotates head B’s query from head A’s direction toward the second key component. Compare the two actual weight distributions. Then change the final projection coefficients and watch how the two payload mixtures combine. The separate value payloads remind us that each head also has its own value projection.

assumptions: The river/bank/loan numbers are an invented geometric example, not an analysis of named linguistic roles in trained attention heads.
The paper uses eight heads with 64-dimensional key/value spaces in its base configuration. This toy shows two heads and scalar output payloads.
The adjustable query direction and output coefficients stand in for learned linear projections. They are not trained inside this scene.
At zero separation the weighting patterns coincide, while outputs may still differ because the value projections are different.

controls.label: Head B view: same direction to second component
Final projection coefficient for head A
Final projection coefficient for head B

objects.text: Same input positions. Different learned views. Parallel mixtures.
Toy token keys: river [2,0]     bank [1,1]     loan [0,2]
Output projection: {{mixA:1}} × head A + {{mixB:1}} × head B = {{projected:3}}

steps.title: Compare the views
steps.text: Head A favors the first component of the toy keys. At full separation, head B favors the second.

steps.title: Keep separate payloads
steps.text: Each head calculates its own weighted value. Concatenation preserves them side by side rather than averaging them immediately.

steps.title: Project the combined result
steps.text: The final learned projection decides how the separate outputs contribute to the next representation. Try identical weighting patterns and different payload projections.

scenes.title: Give each position a usable numerical signature
scenes.explanation: Attention needs information about sequence order. This paper adds a positional vector to each token embedding, using paired sine and cosine waves at several frequencies. A pair is like a clock hand: shifting position rotates it. The scene computes the paper’s formula directly, using a small eight-dimensional example with four frequency pairs. Play moves the active position by the selected offset. The second readout recomputes the same pair as a linear combination of its original sine and cosine values. This is the fixed-offset property the authors discuss. Adding these values to an embedding makes position available to later learned operations; it does not force the model to use position correctly.

assumptions: This illustration uses d_model=8 so that four frequency pairs can be explored. The paper’s base model uses d_model=512.
The two displayed embedding components are invented values, not learned embeddings from the paper.
Only one sine/cosine pair is shown at a time; a full positional vector concatenates pairs at different frequencies.
The authors motivate possible extrapolation to longer sequences and report similar results with learned positions. The display is not evidence of unlimited length generalization.

objects.text: Order becomes a numeric pattern added to each token vector.
Play moves from the base position to base + offset. Select another frequency pair.

steps.title: Start from a position
steps.text: The gray arrow marks the base position in this frequency pair. Other pairs use different wavelengths.

steps.title: Move by an offset
steps.text: The active position rotates the pair. The sine and cosine traces show the same values against sequence position.

steps.title: Translate a relative displacement
steps.text: Compare the direct formula with the rotation readout. A fixed positional offset is a linear transformation of the original pair; learned attention can use that structure.
